title: Judgment on Israel's Cruel Neighbors
overview: Amos announces that God will judge the nations around Israel for brutal acts of war, building toward a shock turn against Judah and Israel themselves in the next chapter.

parts.label: Who Amos was and when (v. 1)
parts.note: Amos was a herder from Tekoa, a village in the southern kingdom of Judah, sent to speak to the northern kingdom of Israel during a prosperous time when both kingdoms had strong kings. Dating his message to two years before the earthquake points to a quake so severe it was still remembered long after.

parts.label: The lion roars (v. 2)
parts.note: God's voice is pictured as a lion's roar from Jerusalem, a warning that danger is near. Even Carmel, a famously green mountain on the coast, dries up, so the whole land will feel it.

parts.label: Damascus and Aram (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: The repeated formula that counts sins as three, then four, is a Hebrew way of saying sin upon sin, though readers differ on whether the one crime then named is the last straw or simply the clearest example. Damascus, capital of Aram (roughly modern Syria), had crushed Gilead, Israelite land east of the Jordan River, as brutally as iron threshing tools crush grain, so its rulers would fall and its people go into exile.

parts.label: Gaza and Tyre sell captives (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: The Philistine cities on the southern coast and the trading city of Tyre rounded up whole communities and sold them as slaves to Edom, and the fire promised against them stands for the flames of war. Tyre also broke a pact of brotherhood, possibly its old alliance with Israel's early kings David and Solomon, though that link is a likely guess rather than certain.

parts.label: Edom turns on kin (vv. 11-12)
parts.note: Edom's people were seen as Israel's relatives, descended from Esau, the brother of Israel's ancestor Jacob. They are charged with hunting their own kin with the sword and nursing a rage that never cooled, and Teman and Bozrah were their main towns.

parts.label: Ammon's atrocity (vv. 13-15)
parts.note: Ammon, east of the Jordan, is accused of cutting open pregnant women in Gilead simply to grab more land. The text names this horror plainly, and the sentence is the burning of its capital Rabbah and exile for its king and officials.

think: Amos condemns these nations for cruelty in war, not for their religion; do you think some wrongs are wrong for every people, whatever they believe, and if so, where does that sense come from?
